title: Improving the Bounds on Approximating Weighted Maximin Share for Chores
summary: We investigate the problem of allocating indivisible chores among agents with arbitrary positive weights and additive nonnegative cost functions. An allocation is said to be $α$-weighted-maximin-share (WMMS) fair if the cost incurred by each agent is at most $α$ times her weighted maximin share. We establish that every instance admits a $4.124234528$-WMMS allocation. Moreover, for instances in which all weights and costs are rational numbers represented in binary, we give an algorithm that computes a $4.12424$-WMMS allocation in time polynomial in the number of agents, the number of chores, and the total binary encoding length of the input. Complementing these upper bounds, we construct a family of instances with strictly positive, identically ordered costs for which the optimal WMMS approximation factors converge to $e$. Together, our results substantially narrow the previously best-known gap of $[2,12]$ established by Li et al.~\cite{LWX26} to $[e,4.12424]$.

title: FirstFit coloring process of random bipartite graphs and an online coloring lower bound in the random order model
summary: FirstFit colors each arriving vertex with the smallest positive integer absent from its previously colored neighborhood. We prove that this rule can require $n^{Ω(1)}$ many colors on certain bipartite graph of $n$ vertices even when the vertices arrive in a uniformly random order. This refutes the conjecture of Bosek, Gutowski, Lasoń, and Przybyło [BGLP24] that FirstFit uses a polylogarithmic expected number of colors on every bipartite graph in the random order model. We obtain the lower bound by analyzing the FirstFit coloring process on random bipartite graphs, where vertices arrive to either side with equal probability, and with an independent edge density $n^{-x}$ for some $0 < x < 1$. Our result can also be viewed as a qualitative strengthening of Kučera [Kuč91], who showed that, for every $ε> 0$, there are graphs with chromatic number at most $n^ε$ on which FirstFit uses $Ω(n/\log n)$ colors in expectation under a uniformly random order. Our result shows that such poor behavior of FirstFit already occurs for $χ(G) = 2$.

title: Faithful Query Resolution for Conversational Search
summary: Conversational query rewriting makes context-dependent requests explicit for retrieval, but additional context can introduce an information need the user did not express. This raises a question about the interaction between query fidelity and retrieval breadth. This paper examines that interaction in behavior-adaptive conversational search, using iKAT SCAI 2026 as the evaluation setting. We compare five query-generation configurations within a behavior-adaptive assistant using BM25 and SPLADE retrieval. A minimal-faithful resolver preserves the user's wording and resolves only context-dependent references; weighted reciprocal rank fusion combines its rankings with those from a learned rewriter and the raw utterance. Offline evaluation shows that adding these formulations recovers recall over the faithful query alone, with a slight reduction in nDCG@10. Across our five iKAT SCAI 2026 submissions, the weighted configuration obtains the highest mean retrieval scores, reaching nDCG@5 of 0.534, a 5.3\% relative improvement over the strongest alternative. However, this retrieval advantage does not coincide with the highest conversational satisfaction scores. These findings motivate separating faithful query interpretation from retrieval expansion, while assessing their effects on conversational utility independently.

title: Sum Rate Maximization for Practical RIS-Enhanced Rate-Splitting Multiple Access Systems
summary: Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) combined with rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) provide a promising solution for improving the spectral efficiency (SE) of sixth-generation (6G) communication systems. However, most existing studies neglect the practical coupling between the RIS phase shift and amplitude, which may cause phase-shift mismatch and significant performance loss. In this paper, we investigate the multiuser sum-rate maximization problem for practical RIS-enhanced RSMA systems considering amplitude-phase coupling. To address the resulting non-convex problem, an effective variable separation algorithm is proposed. The proposed algorithm is compatible with RIS reflecting optimization under the continuous phase shift or any amplitude-phase coupling relationship and can also be directly extended to practical RIS-enhanced NOMA and OMA systems. Simulation results demonstrate performance gain of over 190\% compared with the ideal-RIS-based benchmark, while the proposed RSMA scheme significantly outperforms the corresponding NOMA and OMA schemes.

title: Fair Allocation with Dichotomous Preferences over Item Complements
summary:
We study the problem of fair allocation when agents have dichotomous submodular preferences over groups of, rather than individual, items. These preferences naturally extend existing models, and have a natural interpretation in settings such as course allocation. We show that this seemingly minor extension results in computational intractability barriers: computing a utilitarian or Nash-optimal allocation with item complements is NP-hard. However, when agents' complementary bundles have size at most $k$, there exist poly-time algorithms that compute $\frac1k$-\maxUSW allocations and approximate Nash-welfare-maximizing allocations. While PO+EF-1 allocations may not exist in the complementary preference setting, it is possible to compute $\frac1{k+1}$-approximately \maxUSW EF-X allocations in polynomial time; furthermore, these allocations offer each agent $i$ a utility of at least $\frac{\MMS_i - k}{k+1 + \frac1n}$, where $\MMS_i$ is agent $i$'s maximin share guarantee.
  While the standard dichotomous binary submodular setting admits simple sequential techniques for computing fair and efficient allocations, our results for the complements setting require more complex tools from combinatorial optimization.

title: Approximation Algorithms for Dual-Memory Request Scheduling in Disaggregated LLM Inference
summary: Disaggregated LLM inference executes the prefill and decode phases on separate resource pools, reducing interference between the two phases. However, this architecture introduces a coupled scheduling problem because a request that completes prefill retains its prompt KV cache in prefill memory until it is admitted to the decode pool. Prefill and decode admission decisions therefore jointly determine memory occupancy and request completion times. To the best of our knowledge, this problem lacks a formal formulation, and no approximation guarantees are known for request scheduling in disaggregated LLM inference. We formalize this setting as the dual-memory request scheduling (DMRS) problem, whose objective is to minimize the sum of request completion times, and prove that it is strongly NP-hard. We develop two deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithms. The first applies to instances satisfying $α<1$ and $β<1$ and achieves an approximation ratio of $8+\frac{4}{1-α}+\frac{8}{1-β}$, where $α$ and $β$ are the maximum normalized prefill and peak decode memory demands among all requests, respectively. In particular, it yields a $32$-approximation when $α,β\leq 1/2$. The second algorithm applies to all feasible instances and achieves a uniform $36$-approximation. Finally, evaluations on two H100 GPUs using trace-derived offline workloads show that the proposed algorithms reduce the sum of request completion times relative to multiple vLLM deployment baselines.

title: Retrieving Complementary Evidence for Multi-Hop RAG with Semantic Gain Graphs
summary: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires finding documents whose evidence is useful in combination. Query relevance and graph connectivity help locate related content, but neither directly measures the additional information one document contributes given another. We introduce SG$^2$RAG, a framework that represents this complementarity through semantic gain. Offline, a large language model assesses the relevant and nonredundant information contributed by one chunk given another within neighborhoods proposed by semantic similarity. These ordered assessments are aggregated into symmetric edge weights to construct a reusable Semantic Gain Graph. Online, controlled Personalized PageRank starts from query-relevant seeds and ranks complementary evidence beyond the initial retrieval set. Experiments on MuSiQue, 2Wiki, and HotpotQA with two language model backbones show that SG$^2$RAG achieves the best average EM, F1, and Recall@10 among the evaluated single-retrieval methods. Under identical candidate support and propagation, semantic gain improves average F1 and Recall@10 over similarity weighting by 4.08 and 4.31 points. Analyses of supporting documents and improvements in three iterative retrieval frameworks further support its effectiveness as a reusable retrieval component.

title: MSE Minimization for Movable Antenna Enhanced Wireless Sensing via Array Geometry Optimization
summary: This paper develops adaptive movable-antenna (MA) array structures to enhance wireless sensing performance under arbitrary SNR conditions, using the AoA estimation MSE as the sensing metric. Due to the presence of strong sidelobes in the ambiguity function of sparse MA arrays, the classical CRB of AoA estimation MSE fails to characterize the true MSE in the low and medium SNR regimes, rendering CRB-optimized antenna position vector designs suboptimal for MA-enabled sensing. We derive a deterministic MSE approximation that captures the local estimation error within the mainlobe of the ambiguity function and the outlier error induced by sidelobes, providing a tractable and accurate optimization objective. We then propose three adaptive MA structures that are tailored to different hardware and computational requirements. For systems with fully independent motors, a movable free array is optimized by a two-stage greedy algorithm, which approaches the performance of the globally optimal exhaustive search but with lower computational complexity. Halving the required motors, a movable nested array fixes the dense inner subarray and adjusts only the outer-subarray spacing, reducing the optimization to a one-dimensional search. As the most hardware-efficient design, a movable twin array is proposed to adjust the inter-subarray spacing only with a single motor, while still achieving significant MSE reduction over fixed array geometries. Numerical results show that the derived approximation closely matches the true MSE compared with existing performance bounds, and that the proposed structures outperform the CRB-optimized designs by orders of magnitude in MSE across the tested low-to-medium SNR range. Moreover, it reveals that in the low-SNR regime, APV reconfiguration is more effective for improving estimation accuracy than simply increasing the number of fixed antennas.

title: The Voter Model with Opinion Graph
comment: Abstract shortened to comply Arxiv requirements
summary:
We study the \emph{voter model with opinion graph}, a generalization of the standard (pull) voter model that adds a notion of bounded confidence. In this process, we consider a finite set $A$ of $n$ agents. Each agent $u \in A$ has an opinion $x_u \in O$, where we model opinions as vertices in an undirected opinion graph $G = (O,E)$ with $|O|=q$. In each step, an agent $u$ interacts with another agent $v \in A$. In contrast to classical voting, $u$ adopts the opinion $x_v$ if and only if $x_v$ and $x_u$ are neighbors in $G$. The process is stable once all remaining opinions are an independent set in $G$. We analyze two variants of the process: the ordinary EdgeVOG process, which samples a pair of interacting agents uniformly at random from all possible pairs, and the productive EdgeVOG process, which samples only pairs with neighboring opinions in $G$.
  We show the following:
  - For every opinion graph and every initial configuration, ordinary EdgeVOG stabilizes within $O(n^2\log n)$ steps in expectation and with high probability. The expectation bound is asymptotically tight. For the productive EdgeVOG process, the expected stabilization time is exactly the initial number of compatible agent pairs, while $O(n^2\log n)$ steps suffice with high probability.
  - An opinion $i$ with initial support $s_i$ survives with probability at least $p_i:=s_i/(s_i+\sum_{j\in N(i)}s_j)$. Further, let $μ= \sum_{i \in O} p_i$, then we show the probability that less than $(1-δ)μ$ opinions survive is at most $\exp(-δ^2μ/(2(Δ^2+1)))$ for every $0\leqδ\leq1$.
  -If $G$ has maximum degree $Δ$ and every opinion initially has support at most $\hat{s}$, then no opinion ever acquires more than $\tilde{O}(\min\{n,Δ^6\hat{s}\})$ agents with high probability. This yields near-linear stabilization bounds for productive EdgeVOG for a large class of configurations.

title: Almost Lossless Transfer for Cuttable Distributed Problems
summary: We study constant-round LOCAL approximation for additive local vertex-subset minimization problems. Given a $k$-uniform $α$-approximation on a hereditary source class closed under disjoint union, Bonamy, Das, Gavoille, Picavet, Suomela, and Wesolek obtained ratio $α(d+1)+1$ on locally nice target classes of asymptotic dimension $d$. We prove two transfers with ratios $α+1+η$ and $α+η$ for every $η>0$. These bounds require the stronger local niceness assumption at a larger scale that depends on $η$. The first algorithm keeps their repair construction and increases the radius used to detect errors. We average over partitions of the graph to bound the retained cost without the factor $d+1$. These partitions are used only in the analysis. The second algorithm tests several deletion widths around the errors. In each component of the repair zone, it chooses a smallest union of retained choices and an exact repair. Averaging over the widths bounds the cost counted twice and yields ratio $α+η$. Both transfers are deterministic and computable, use arbitrary distinct numerical identifiers, and need no knowledge of the graph size. Their outputs also satisfy local uniformity guarantees. For 2-domination on graphs of bounded Euler genus, the same planar source gives ratio $19$ through the earlier transfer and $6+η$ through ours. For minimum dominating set, our transfer gives ratio $7+\varepsilon$ on graphs formed by attaching a clique of arbitrary size at one vertex of a planar graph, using the source algorithm of Amiri and Siebertz. This class satisfies our target assumptions and allows nonempty error sets. Its Euler genus is unbounded, so their guarantee for graphs of bounded Euler genus does not cover the whole class.

title: Understanding ChatGPT Citations: Evidence from Production Web Search Across Model Generations
summary: Generative engines such as ChatGPT Web retrieve webpages to answer user queries, but only a subset are shown as citations. Understanding this retrieval-to-citation process is important for generative engine optimization (GEO), which aims to improve content visibility in generative-engine responses. However, prior studies mainly analyze final responses, leaving the internal execution process and its variation across model settings less understood. To this end, we conduct an observational study of four ChatGPT Web settings from ChatGPT 5.2 to 5.5, covering Instant and Thinking modes at the URL, hostname, and entity levels. We examine how ChatGPT rewrites queries, retrieves candidate webpages, and selects references. The Instant settings remain mostly single-round, while GPT-5.4 Thinking frequently performs multiple retrieval rounds. Across repeated runs, candidates retrieved more often are also more likely to be cited. We then evaluate Google Search and the OpenAI Responses API as external proxies. Responses API candidates provide broader coverage, while its citations more closely match sources cited by ChatGPT Web. Both proxies match ChatGPT Web better at the hostname and entity levels than at the exact-URL level. Even when combined, they recover only about one quarter of cited URLs. We further test whether these external signals remain predictive when combined. Within the external candidate set, a supervised model combining them reaches AUCs above 0.74 for GPT-5.3 and GPT-5.5 at all three levels. These findings suggest that GEO should distinguish retrieval visibility from citation visibility, account for rewritten queries and run-to-run variation, and consider hostname- and entity-level presence in addition to exact URLs. Differences across settings also suggest that GEO strategies should be re-evaluated when the deployed setting or serving environment changes.

title: Effective DoF Collapse in Sparse Near-Field Beamforming: A Block-Rank-1 Mechanism
comment: This paper(2-column version) has been accept for publish in IEEE wireless communication letter(WCL)
summary: Sparse near-field arrays phase-cohere $M$ widely separated sub-arrays of $N$ elements and underpin distributed MIMO, satellite formations, and integrated sensing and communication. We show that their interference suppression over a protected region is set by coherence within a single sub-array rather than by the span of the formation: the effective rank of the region covariance can collapse from $MN$ to $M$. Two independent arguments establish this. For canonical line and disk regions each diagonal covariance block is exactly a classical concentration operator, which supplies sharp per-block rank thresholds and makes fewer than one spatial degree of freedom per sub-array a conservative design rule; an orthogonal decomposition with eigenvalue interlacing gives a nonasymptotic sufficient condition that assumes nothing about the coupling between platforms. The consequences are covariance-side and beamformer-independent: the unloaded Capon functional upper-bounds worst-case signal-to-interference ratio, while its regularized counterpart scales very differently for angularly separated and for in-cone targets. An eight-satellite LEO study validates the theory, including realized worst-case SIR.

title: The Complexity of Exact and Approximate Nash Equilibria in Anonymous Games
comment: 48 pages, including appendices and references; 2 figures and 4 tables
summary: We prove that, for every fixed rational $c>0$, computing a $2^{-n^c}$-approximate Nash equilibrium in an $n$-player two-strategy anonymous game is $\mathsf{PPAD}$-complete. This holds even when one strategy always pays $1/2$ and, for all but two players, the other is constant outside at most five opponent counts. The reduction uses coefficient estimates to simulate circuit constraints approximately. Exact computation requires eliminating the simulation error: with three strategies, a separate construction uses polynomial roots to implement circuit gates exactly. This yields $\mathsf{FIXP}$-completeness of exact equilibrium computation under separable-linear reductions and $\mathsf{FIXP}_a$-completeness of approximation in distance to an exact equilibrium.

title: Metric Planarity Testing is Hard
summary:
A key milestone in algorithmic graph theory is Hopcroft and Tarjan's 1974 linear-time algorithm for graph planarity testing. At a workshop in 2002, Linial and Rabinovich asked for either a polynomial-time algorithm or an NP-hardness proof for metric planarity testing: given a metric space $(X,d_X)$, determine whether there exists an edge-weighted planar graph $G=(V,E,w)$ with $X\subseteq V$ that realizes the distances in $X$, meaning that $d_G(x,y)=d_X(x,y)$ for every $x,y\in X$. This question arose in the context of research on metric embeddings and their applications in computer science since the mid-1990s. Over the past few decades, polynomial-time algorithms have been developed for several special cases.
  In this work, we show that metric planarity testing is NP-hard, in sharp contrast to graph planarity testing. Our reduction yields a stronger result: under the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), no $2^{o(n)}$-time algorithm for metric planarity testing exists, where $n$ is the number of points in the metric.
  To complement our ETH lower bound, we give two algorithmic results: (i) an algorithm for computing a metric planar embedding in $2^{\tilde{O}(n^2)}$ time and (ii) a $(1+ε)$-approximation algorithm in $2^{\tilde{O}(n)}$ time for any fixed $ε\in(0,1)$. The second algorithm produces a planar graph that preserves the input metric up to a factor of $(1+ε)$.

title: Toward Explainability in Multimodal Recommendation
summary: Multimodal recommender systems effectively alleviate data sparsity and cold-start problems by integrating heterogeneous information, yet complex cross-modal representations and model decision-making processes also introduce new interpretability challenges. Despite the rapid growth of research on the interpretability of multimodal recommendation in recent years, relevant methods and evaluation criteria remain relatively fragmented, lacking a unified conceptual framework. To address this gap, this paper categorizes existing methods into modality explanation and post-hoc explanation based on the timing and manner of explanation generation, and further constructs a progressive system for each category. Building on this foundation, this paper synthesizes four categories of evaluation metrics from both objective quantitative and subjective perceptual perspectives, and reviews relevant datasets along the dimensions of application domain and data source. Through a comprehensive analysis of existing research, we further propose future research directions. This paper aims to establish a unified analytical perspective across multimodal representation, recommendation decision-making, and user preferences, providing a research foundation for building transparent and trustworthy multimodal recommender systems.

title: Entropy/Length Profile Bounds for the Conversion of (Non)linear Codes in the Merge Regime
summary: Code conversion changes the parameters of encoded data while avoiding complete decoding and re-encoding. Existing general bounds largely rely on the algebraic structure of linear codes. This paper develops an information-theoretic framework for nonlinear code conversion in the merge regime. Using the entropy/length profile (ELP), we derive upper bounds on the number of unchanged symbols and lower bounds on the number of read symbols for arbitrary $(n,M)_q$ codes, without assuming linearity or requiring $\log_q M$ to be an integer. We also obtain joint bounds for multiple initial codes and consequences involving minimum distance. For linear codes, the proposed bounds reduce to the corresponding generalized Hamming weight (GHW) bounds. The construction based on Hamming codes converts Hamming codes of redundancy two into a Hamming code of any larger redundancy and simultaneously attains the general bounds on unchanged and read symbols. The construction based on quasigroups shows that new bounds remain tight for genuinely nonlinear codes of nonintegral dimension and at a nonintegral entropy threshold, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first construction of convertible codes for nonlinear codes.

title: Online Fair Division with Upgrade Recourse
summary: We study the online fair division of indivisible goods. In the standard model, where assignments are irrevocable, no algorithm can guarantee any positive fraction of the maximin share (MMS). Reassigning earlier goods can restore fairness, but it may take value away from agents who already hold them. We ask how much fairness can be maintained if every reassignment must leave each affected agent at least as well off. We consider two forms of such upgrade recourse. Under item-level upgrades, each good an agent holds must be kept or replaced by a distinct good she values at least as much; under bundle-level upgrades, only her total value must not decrease. For item-level upgrades, we show that the optimal MMS factor is essentially $1/H_n \approx 1/\ln n$, where $H_n$ is the $n$-th harmonic number, and that fixed picking sequences nearly attain it. Since these sequences use only the agents' rankings of individual goods, knowing the actual values cannot improve the optimal factor for up to 33 agents, and improves it by at most a vanishing margin as $n$ grows. Bundle-level upgrades allow substantially stronger guarantees. By permitting several-for-one exchanges, they turn this vanishing factor into a constant: we achieve exact MMS for two agents and more than half of MMS for any number of agents, in both cases together with relaxations of envy-freeness. Finally, we show that predictions about future goods let online algorithms inherit any offline MMS guarantee, losing only an additive term bounded by the prediction error. Under item-level upgrades, however, insisting on exact MMS when predictions are correct leaves no positive guarantee when they are wrong.

title: Exact and Asymptotic Analysis of Greedy Online Facility Assignment on Cycle Metrics
summary: We identify the free-facility gaps of greedy online assignment on a cycle with the discrete additive coalescent and use this connection to determine the exact expected assignment cost. The cycle has circumference $n$, with one unit-capacity facility at each integer point and $n$ independent uniform arrivals. Each request is assigned immediately to a nearest free facility. The conditional one-step cost is the sum of squared gap lengths divided by $4n$. A uniform cyclic-order argument identifies the unordered gap process with additive coalescence. The classical Cayley-tree representation then reduces the accumulated cost to a two-vertex distance functional, yielding \[ G_n=\frac n4\sum_{d=0}^{n-1}\prod_{j=1}^{d}\left(1-\frac jn\right) \sim\frac14\sqrt{\frac\pi2}\,n^{3/2}. \] The formula requires a linear number of scalar recurrence steps to evaluate. We also obtain an asymptotic upper bound of $π\sqrt3/2$ on the ratio of expected greedy cost to expected offline optimum under this arrival model. An exact rational Bellman calculation shows that greedy is optimal for three facilities but exceeds the optimal online expected cost by $1/512$ for four facilities. Independent exact recurrences and finite tree enumeration provide reproducible checks of the analysis.

title: Federated Semantic Residuals for Multimodal Recommendation
summary: Federated Recommendation Systems (FedRSs) learn collaborative scores from interaction histories on device and rank items by them, so a higher score means a higher rank. Item text and images add semantic information that can reorder the list. Existing Federated Multimodal Recommenders (FedMRs) fuse this content into their models, which can obscure how content reorders the list. We therefore propose the SEmantic Residual Adapter (SERA), which keeps content out of an existing FedRS and adds semantic residual scores to its collaborative scores. Content can then lift an item above another only when its semantic residual score exceeds the other's by more than their collaborative score gap. This score grows with the item's content similarity to the user's interaction history and is capped at a residual bound. We prove that for any content, an item can enter the list only if its collaborative score is within twice this bound of the lowest one in the list. A larger bound lets content lift more items, including irrelevant ones, so the bound trades off how far content reaches against accuracy. With a validated bound, SERA improves all three FedRSs on all six datasets without adding personalized parameters. It outperforms FedMRs in most comparisons and lifts some FedRSs above centralized baselines.

title: Rydberg Atomic Quantum Receivers for OFDM Systems: An Atomic-Comb Design
comment: This manuscript has been submitted to IEEE journal
summary: Rydberg atomic quantum receivers (RAQR) exhibit exceptional sensitivity to radio-frequency (RF) signals, positioning them as promising candidates for next-generation wireless systems. Extending their capabilities to orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM), however, requires atomic responses that go beyond broadband reception and are tailored to the structured interference of multicarrier signals. To bridge this gap, we develop an atomic-comb Rydberg receiver based on six-wave mixing (SWM) transduction. In particular, injecting a multi-tone local oscillator (LO) into the RAQR generates frequency-shifted replicas of the intrinsic SWM response. By subtly tuning the amplitude and phase of each LO tone, constructive and destructive interference can be selectively induced to preserve desired response components while attenuating harmful frequency offsets. Furthermore, we harness the response-reshaping capability of the proposed atomic comb to proactively mitigate OFDM interference. More explicitly, by exploiting the discrete difference-frequency structure of both carrier-frequency-offset (CFO)-induced and phase-noise (PN)-induced inter-carrier interference (ICI), we optimize the atomic-comb response to suppress dominant ICI components directly. We further reveal an intrinsic coupling between spectral shaping and the time-domain effective channel memory, motivating a joint optimization of both ICI and inter-symbol interference (ISI), which simultaneously suppresses inter-carrier leakage and post-cyclic-prefix (CP) tail energy. Extensive simulation results validate our atomic-comb design, unveiling that the proposed atomic comb can effectively reshape the receiver response over the OFDM, while mitigating ICI, shortening the effective channel memory, and substantially lowering CP overhead.

title: An Introduction to Contract Theory for Computer Scientists
summary: This survey introduces contract design to computer scientists: using outcome-based payments to incentivize effort. We discuss applications that motivate a computational approach to contract design, ranging from online labor markets, to incentive-aware algorithmic classification, to emerging ecosystems of AI agents. We present the classic principal-agent model and introduce basic concepts. We show how optimal contracts are computable via linear programming, and why they can be opaque and brittle. Motivated by this we turn to simpler contract formats, specifically linear contracts. We discuss approximation guarantees, and robust (max-min) optimality of such contracts. We then move beyond the single-agent setting to combinatorial contract settings with multiple agents, mapping the algorithmic landscape of tractability and approximation. Finally, we discuss partial information settings through the lens of learning algorithms, and outline open directions. The goal is a concise, accessible entry point that connects economic foundations with algorithmic tools and highlights opportunities for new theory and applications.

title: Adaptive Sorting, also in the BST Model
summary:
Sorting is one of the most basic algorithmic problems. Adaptive sorting algorithms exploit features that make an input easier to sort, often captured by entropy measures. Many such measures have been studied, raising two natural questions: how do they relate to one another, and are there algorithms that are adaptive to them?
  We complete a hierarchy of relations between previously studied entropy measures and show that the classical measure Reg is a source of this hierarchy. We prove that an existing data structure yields a Reg-adaptive sorting algorithm, thereby achieving the adaptive bounds of every measure in the hierarchy. Following McIlroy's observation that Reg has a mathematically inconvenient definition, we study a slightly weaker but simpler measure, reg. For inputs without duplicates, we show that O(n + log reg) = O(n + log Reg), so this simplification preserves the adaptive bound.
  Finally, we do algorithms design and introduce SproutSort, a reg-adaptive algorithm in the offline binary search tree (BST) model. SproutSort achieves an access cost of O(n + log reg), making it the most adaptive algorithm in this model to date. We also introduce SkeletonSort, a simple randomised pointer-machine algorithm that sorts distinct keys in expected O(n + log reg) time, offering a considerably simpler implementation of a sorting algorithm this high in the adaptive hierarchy.

title: Pathwise Alignment for Collaborative Filtering: Bilateral Conditional Flow Regularization
summary: Collaborative filtering predicts user-item interactions from implicit feedback. We focus on matrix factorization (MF) trained with the Bayesian Personalized Ranking loss. This loss updates each user embedding only through that user's observed items and sampled negatives, so sparse feedback gives MF few constraints. To constrain each user through other users, we propose Pathwise Alignment for Collaborative Filtering (PACF), which trains MF with one network shared by all training pairs. At points between user and item embeddings, a flow matching term trains the network to predict the user-to-item step, reversed and scaled for sampled negatives. A trajectory consistency term pulls each user's predicted path to end at the observed item. Both terms update the embeddings, so the network is discarded after training, thereby maintaining the efficiency of MF at inference. We prove that a network with bounded sensitivity to its input point accurately fits users who share an item only if their embeddings are close, so these users constrain one another. Against eleven discriminative and generative baselines, PACF achieves the highest performance on all seven datasets. Its relative gains over MF are largest where feedback is sparsest. The shared network thus supplies the missing constraints through other users.

title: New Minimum Storage Regenerating Codes With Small Sub-packetization Levels for All Admissible Repair Degrees
summary: In this paper, {we propose a new family of $(n, k)$ Minimum Storage Regenerating (MSR) codes} for distributed storage systems. By structuring the parity-check matrix as a block Vandermonde matrix composed of diagonal matrices and generalized permutation matrices, the proposed code achieves a sub-packetization level of $N = (d-k+1)^{\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil}$ and supports any repair degree $k+1\le d<n$. A key innovation of the new construction lies in relaxing the strict commutativity condition previously required for the building blocks in the parity-check matrices of Ye-Barg codes. We introduce a novel proof technique to establish the MDS property without relying on full commutativity, thereby generalizing the applicability of block Vandermonde matrices and enriching the family of Ye-Barg codes. Additionally, the sparsity of the parity-check matrix enhances encoding and decoding efficiency by reducing computational complexity. This work provides new insights into the construction of MSR codes.

title: Dynamic Run-Out Pricing for Perishable Goods
summary:
I study a dynamic pricing problem in which a seller with limited inventory must sequentially price a perishable product for arriving customers with heterogeneous valuations. The key difficulty lies in balancing immediate sales against future opportunities under capacity constraints and stochastic customer valuations. I propose a simple, interpretable, and asymptotically optimal dynamic pricing algorithm, called Dynamic Run-Out Pricing (DROP), that adjusts prices in real time based on current inventory and anticipated future demand.
  Under the assumption that customers' valuations follow bounded or exponential distributions, our theoretical results show that DROP's expected revenue converges to the optimal revenue as market size grows. Unlike traditional notions of near-optimality, where the ratio of the algorithm's revenue to the optimal revenue converges to 1, I show that the absolute difference between the two revenues converges to 0 as the market size increases, underscoring the algorithm's effectiveness.
  Furthermore, I extend our analysis to heavy-tailed valuation distributions, specifically the Pareto distribution, where standard run-out heuristics severely underprice inventory by ignoring the value of waiting for extreme valuations. To correct this, I introduce the Tail-Aware DROP (TA-DROP) heuristic, which intentionally inflates prices to protect inventory, and I prove that it restores asymptotic optimality with a strict polynomial convergence rate.

title: Social Learning of Ranking: Getting the Top Right despite Local Herding
summary:
In sequential learning, a group of agents sequentially receives a noisy private signal and observes the predictions of prior agents to estimate a hidden ground truth. While extensively studied for binary signals, we formalize and analyze sequential learning when the hidden ground truth is an ordering of $n$ items, and both private signals and inferences involve pairwise comparisons.
  A key focus in sequential learning is herding, where agents disregard their private signals to follow the crowd. We show that, while local herding in our model may lead agents to make incorrect pairwise inferences, the global hidden order can still be approximated. Specifically, by aggregating all pairwise comparison outputs, the highest-ranked items can be retrieved. We investigate top-$k$ retrieval across three scenarios: (1) passive aggregation, where information is gathered from the social learning process without intervention; (2) strategic selection, where agents choose their pairwise comparisons dynamically; and (3) aggregation with stubborn nodes, where a very small set of stubborn agents, who base their inferences solely on their private signals, join the mechanism. With query complexity as the number of agents needed for a high-probability estimation, we propose top-$k$ retrieval algorithms with query complexities sublinear in $O(n^2)$, the total number of pairs.

title: Rethinking Evidence Modeling: Context-Coupled Graph Learning for Multimodal Recommendation
summary: Multimodal graph recommendation integrates observed interactions with item images and text to learn user preferences. These inputs constitute Semantic-Behavioral Evidence (SBE). Many existing graph methods incorporate collaborative and multimodal semantic relations, yet their aggregation and state updates remain context-separated, limiting the continuous composition of preference evidence across layers and the joint use of multiple sources. To address this limitation, we propose CC-MGRec, a context-coupled graph learning method that organizes SBE within a common graph learning context for cross-relation modeling and compositional propagation. Its context-coupled multimodal graph integrates user-item collaborative relations and item-item semantic relations, coordinating their message scales through joint normalization. Recommendation-grounded semantic calibration uses training behavior to adjust semantic neighbor weights while preserving normalized collaborative propagation coefficients. Collaborative-semantic compositional propagation updates shared node states layer by layer to continuously compose collaborative and multimodal semantic evidence, implicitly forming Preference Evidence Chains (PECs), including collaborative-semantic and visual-textual PECs. Joint execution of relation messages on the same shared node states within each layer preserves propagation outputs while reducing intermediate output processing and fusion overhead. We provide theoretical analysis of the proposed mechanisms. Experiments on three Amazon datasets demonstrate improved recommendation quality and faster inference during graph propagation.

title: Wyner's Common Information and the Common Entropy are NP-Hard to Compute
comment: A preliminary version of the manuscript
summary: Wyner's common information $J(p)$ and the common entropy $G(p)$ of a pair of random variables $(X,Y)$ with finite ranges and joint distribution $p$ are both defined by an optimization over the auxiliary random variables $W$ that make $X$ and $Y$ conditionally independent: $J(p)$ is the infimum of the mutual information $I(X,Y;W)$, and $G(p)$ is the infimum of the entropy $H(W)$. We prove that both quantities are NP-hard to compute. For Wyner's common information, deciding whether $J(p)$ is strictly smaller than a given integer $r$ is NP-hard, and the problem is NP-complete on tables that are uniform on their support and have the same number of positive entries in every row. The reduction is from Maximum Edge Biclique and rests on an exact criterion, in terms of rectangles in the support of $p$, for improving on the auxiliary $W=X$; every yes-instance satisfies $J(p)<r-1/(4N^2)$ and every no-instance satisfies $J(p)=r$, where $N$ is the number of positive entries of $p$. For the common entropy, deciding whether $G(p)\le r$ for a rational number $r$ is NP-hard, even for tables with at most four nonzero entries in each row, all taking one of two values. The reduction is from exact cover by $3$-sets and rests on a majorization property of the masses of the nonnegative rank-one decompositions of $p$, combined with a quantitative form of the Schur concavity of entropy. In both cases the separation between yes- and no-instances is inverse-polynomial in the size of $p$, so that approximating $J(p)$ or $G(p)$ within a suitable inverse-polynomial additive error is also NP-hard. The two mechanisms are genuinely different: we exhibit a table on which a large rectangle in the support lowers $J$ below the threshold of our first reduction while leaving $G$ on it.

title: A Stochastic Growth Model for Online Platforms
summary:
We investigate the growth trajectory of online platforms operating as market makers in two-sided matching markets. Their expansion, often referred to as the ``chicken-and-egg dilemma'' in the literature, poses an inherent challenge: service providers find value in joining the platform because of the presence of customers, while customers are drawn to the platform by the availability of service providers. Much of the existing literature addresses this expansion challenge through either a static market-clearing lens or aggregate dynamic models, emphasizing how network externalities shape a platform's growth trajectory and equilibrium size. These approaches do not fully capture how gradual growth must be implemented through server-level admission, assignment, and compensation decisions. Embedded in this growth process are intertemporal participation constraints that the platform must satisfy to attract and retain forward-looking servers.
  To explicitly account for the stochastic dynamics of a platform's gradual growth, we model the system as a Markov process. Potential servers and customers arrive according to Poisson processes, and customer demand is non-decreasing in the number of active servers. Under mild conditions, we characterize the platform's optimal admission, assignment, and compensation policies. The platform admits servers at the maximum feasible rate until it reaches an endogenous target size, which can be smaller than the static market-clearing optimum. In the baseline model, seniority-based compensation acts as an operational substitute for financially subsidized growth: instead of using upfront subsidies to induce early server participation, the platform uses future cash flows to reward early servers for joining when demand is limited and for helping the platform reach later, higher-demand states.

title: Online Batching with Lookahead: Adversarial Limits and Stochastic Gains
summary:
Modern inference systems rely on batching to exploit parallel execution and amortize serial execution overheads, but batching creates a fundamental online scheduling tradeoff: serving requests immediately reduces request queuing delay, while waiting can form larger batches that better utilize parallel hardware and improve serving efficiency. We study this tradeoff in a single-server online batching model with bounded batch capacity, fixed batch processing time, and the objective of minimizing total flow time. Our focus is on the value of finite lookahead into future arrivals over a purely online setting for scheduling.
  We show that the benefits of lookahead depend on the arrival model. In the adversarial setting, finite perfect lookahead has inherent limitations: for any bounded lookahead window, every online algorithm remains separated from the offline optimum by a constant factor. Thus, worst-case arrival sequences can prevent perfect knowledge of future events from fully overcoming online uncertainty. In contrast, under Poisson arrivals in the stable regime, finite lookahead is much more powerful. Although the best distribution-aware online algorithm has a nonzero asymptotic gap from the offline optimum, lookahead closes this gap exponentially fast in the window length. We prove matching upper and lower bounds up to constants in the exponent. Together, these results give a tight characterization of when lookahead can close the online--offline gap, incorporating insights from the competitive analysis of online algorithms into queueing-theoretic steady-state bounds.
  We also study imperfect predictions, showing that the benefit of lookahead degrades gracefully with prediction error. Simulations on synthetic arrivals and experiments on real request traces support the theory: modest lookahead substantially reduces flow time and brings online batching close to the offline benchmark.

title: Local Citation Recommendation Without Graph Signals
comment: Accepted at WASP 2026, co-located with AACL-IJCNLP 2026. 16 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/adsabs/LCRC Code: https://github.com/benjaminb/citeline
summary: Resolving correct citations can be a time-consuming task for research writers. We address local citation recommendation (LCR), where the goal is to retrieve appropriate references for a given sentence. Web tools generally depend on the existing citation graph, which may bias results toward citation count or more recent publications. LCR research using full paper texts has been limited by the lack of publicly available data. We present a new dataset, the Local Citation Recommendation Corpus (LCRC), containing 14,735 scientific statements derived from astrophysics review papers, each with one or more citation targets whose full text is accessible via API. Using this dataset we systematically compare retrieval methods and develop a citation recommendation system that avoids citation graph bias while achieving 8.0% improvement in Recall@25 and 6.9% improvement in NDCG@25 over dense retrieval baselines without model fine-tuning. To support reproducibility, we make our code and dataset publicly available.

title: Insdel Reed-Solomon Decoding Algorithms up to the Half-Singleton Bound
summary: In this paper, we focus on decoding optimal Reed-Solomon codes of dimension two for insdel errors up to the half-Singleton bound. We present a decoding algorithm for the general insertion-and-deletion scenario with a time complexity smaller than brute-force decoding. Our algorithm corrects insdel errors up to the half-Singleton bound, which exceeds the scope of existing methods. Additionally, for the special cases of insertion-only and deletion-only insdel error patterns, we present two different algorithms with a time complexity smaller than our general algorithm.

title: Unit-Demand Pricing for Min-Buying Customers
summary: We study the unit-demand pricing problem under \textit{min-buying} behavior, where customers purchase the lowest-priced item that yields non-negative utility. In contrast to the quasi-linear model, we show that uniform pricing becomes substantially more effective under min-buying. First, we study symmetric environments. We show that for min-buying customers with independent and identically distributed valuations, a uniform price across items is optimal. We then extend this optimality result to all valuations drawn from exchangeable and affiliated distributions. However, uniform pricing is not optimal in all symmetric environments: for min-buying customers we construct an exchangeable and non-affiliated valuation distribution for which the gap between uniform pricing and optimal item pricing is logarithmic in the number of items. This gap is tight and matches the worst-case gap in the quasi-linear setting. Next, we consider asymmetric environments in which valuations are independent but not identically distributed. When these valuations are regular and customers are min-buying, we show that a uniform price guarantees approximately 69.86\% of the optimal item-pricing revenue and this is tight. Overall, our results highlight that the value of non-uniform pricing substantially diminishes, and often disappears entirely, under more conservative demand models in which customers engage in satisficing behaviors such as min-buying.

title: QPTAS for Max Weight Independent Set in Graphs with Strongly Edge-Sublinear Separators
summary: A hereditary graph class has strongly edge-sublinear separators if, for some constant $0 \leqslant b < 1$, every graph in the class with $m$ edges admits a balanced separator of size $\mathcal O(m^b)$. We show that Max Weight Independent Set (MWIS) admits a deterministic quasipolynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS) on every such class. In particular, this applies to graphs excluding any fixed graph as an induced minor, by a separator theorem of Korhonen and Lokshtanov [SODA 2024]. Our theorem generalizes the QPTASes for axis-parallel rectangles [Adamaszek and Wiese, FOCS 2013] and polygons [Adamaszek, Har-Peled, and Wiese, JACM 2019], or equivalently for packing connected subgraphs of a planar graph [Pilipczuk, van Leeuwen, and Wiese, Algorithmica 2020]. It also generalizes the QPTAS for MWIS on hereditary classes with strongly sublinear separators measured in vertices [Dvořák, EJC 2018; Dvořák and Lahiri, ESA 2021], as well as the QPTASes for graphs excluding particular induced minors [Chudnovsky et al., arXiv 2025; Bonnet et al., SWAT 2026; Czyżewska et al., arXiv 2026].

title: KhyontekAI at CheckThat! 2026: Multilingual Dense Retrieval and Cross-Encoder Reranking for Scientific Web Claims
comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, 9 tables. Author version of the paper published in CEUR Workshop Proceedings, Vol. 4283 (CLEF 2026 Working Notes, Jena, Germany)
summary: Scientific claims shared through social media platforms frequently reference research findings without explicitly linking to the corresponding scientific publications. Automatically retrieving the correct scientific source for such claims is a challenging multilingual retrieval problem involving semantic matching, paraphrasing, noisy social media text, and cross-domain language variation. In this work, we present a multilingual two-stage retrieval framework for CLEF 2026 CheckThat! Task 1 on Source Retrieval for Scientific Web Claims. Our system combines fine-tuned dense retrieval models with cross-encoder reranking for improving multilingual scientific document retrieval. We evaluate multiple transformer-based dense retrieval architectures including multilingual-E5, BGE, and Contriever under different metadata configurations. We further investigate multilingual joint training, retrieval depth analysis, metadata enrichment, and language balancing strategies for improving retrieval effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that metadata enrichment consistently improves retrieval effectiveness, while fine-tuned cross-encoder reranking provides additional gains in retrieval precision. Our final multilingual system achieves MRR@5 scores of 0.6222 for English, 0.5112 for German, and 0.6254 for French, with an overall average MRR@5 score of 0.5862.

title: An Upper Bound to the Undetected Error Exponent with Erasure Decoding at Positive Rates
summary: We study the undetected-error exponent of discrete memoryless channels with erasure decoding. Assuming that the undetected-error and erasure probabilities vanish, we derive an upper bound on the undetected-error exponent at positive rates. The bound uses Somekh-Baruch's genie-aided argument where an auxiliary output provides the decoder with a list of codewords. It recovers Telatar's tight rate-zero converse and is at least as tight as the straight-line bound. A numerical example shows that the improvement over the straight-line bound can be strict.

title: Improved Combinatorial Auctions with and without Samples
comment: Abstract shortened to fit arXiv constraints
summary:
We give new mechanisms for combinatorial auctions in the offline, secretary, and prophet-with-samples models. Specifically, we obtain the following guarantees for social welfare maximization with $m$ items and $n$ XOS buyers:
  * In the prophet-with-samples version, buyers arrive in adversarial order and draw their values from independent distributions. We give a universally truthful, polynomial-time $(2+\eps)$-approximation mechanism using $O(\log\!\log m)$ samples from each distribution. The approximation factor is tight even for a single item and without the incentive constraints, due to the classic prophet inequality. Compared to the previous state-of-the-art with the same guarantees [Dütting--Kesselheim--Lucier--Reiffenhäuser--Singla (FOCS 2024)], our running time is exponentially faster, and our sample complexity is doubly-exponentially lower, resolving two explicit open problems by Dütting et al.
  * Using the same techniques, we also obtain improved mechanisms in the secretary and offline versions, where the values are worst-case, and buyers are processed in either random order (secretary) or without any timing restrictions (offline). After a long line of works, the state of the art in both models is an $O((\log\!\log m)^2)$-approximation due to [Assadi--Kesselheim--Singla (SODA 2021)], who explicitly ask whether it can be improved to $O(\log\!\log m)$. We indeed obtain an $O(\log\!\log m)$-approximate universally truthful mechanism for the secretary and offline models.

title: Stochastic Weighted Caching with Per-Request Predictions
summary:
Both the unweighted and weighted variants of caching are cornerstone problems in competitive analysis, with tight randomized competitive ratios of $Θ(\log k)$, where $k$ is the cache size. We study weighted caching with per-request predictions, where each page request is accompanied by a prediction of the next arrival time of the same page. For unweighted caching, such perfect predictions suffice to implement Belady's offline optimal rule. For weighted caching, however, previous work shows that a logarithmic lower bound persists even with perfect predictions on adversarial request sequences. Stochastic assumptions alone are also insufficient: the classical caching lower bounds already apply to uniform independent requests. In this work, we ask whether combining these two sources of additional information can overcome this barrier, and answer this question affirmatively.
  Specifically, we develop an efficient, deterministic cache eviction policy that achieves a competitive ratio of $15.75$ using perfect per-request predictions when page requests are drawn independently from an arbitrary, known static distribution in every step, and page costs are arbitrary. Our algorithm's performance degrades gracefully under erroneous predictions: we prove a bound of $O(\min\{1+E,\log k\})$ on the competitive ratio, where $E$ aggregates each page's average prediction error, and may be unknown to the algorithm.

title: Personalized LLM Recommendation with Semantic IDs: Autoregressive Beam Search vs. Multi-Token Prediction
summary: Large-scale personalization is shifting from embedding-table retrieval to LLM-based recommenders that generate the Semantic ID (SID) of the item to recommend, where each SID is a short sequence of discrete hierarchical content codes. A single instruction-tuned model can then unify retrieval, content understanding, and language, and recommend brand-new titles from their content alone using SID; then, how should the model generate the SID? Traditionally, models rely on a single language modeling head that generates tokens autoregressively, typically using constrained beam search. In contrast, an emerging body of work explores multi-token prediction (MTP), where dedicated heads predict all tokens in parallel, substantially reducing the decoding latency associated with beam search. We report an industry-scale, apples-to-apples comparison of these two generation paradigms: single-head autoregressive decoding vs. MTP. We introduce a new auxiliary ranking loss, defined over the joint SID score, to train the MTP objective. We evaluate the SID training objectives on both quality and training/inference cost, inside a multi-task LLM that jointly does personalized retrieval, content question-answering (QA), and instruction following over a large streaming-media catalog. Our experiments show single-head beam search consistently beats MTP on most product-critical metrics: ranking and content QA, and trains at roughly 2.6x lower dollar cost on Qwen3-8B scale; MTP wins only on raw inference throughput. Around this finding, we detail an efficient training and inference stack and report end-to-end gains over the previous non-SID baseline equipped with an auxiliary ranking head: +77% item cold-start ranking, +22% content-QA accuracy, +2.8x faster training, with language metric regression traced to SID vocabulary expansion. We address the language regression by reinforcement learning post training.

title: Universal Decoding for Unequal Error Protection
summary: We study universal unequal error protection of a single special message over discrete memoryless channels. We construct a sequence of codes with a decoding rule that does not depend on the channel transition law. We derive an achievable error exponent for the special message while ensuring reliable decoding of the ordinary messages. The resulting exponent strictly improves on the natural equal-error-protection random-coding baseline and remains positive as the rate approaches capacity. For symmetric channels, it converges to the optimal red-alert exponent at capacity.

title: A Matroid Generalization of Weighted Popular Matching: Characterization and Algorithm
summary:
We study a problem that unifies two major generalizations of popular matchings in the one-sided preference model. In a bipartite graph in which each vertex, or applicant, on one side has preferences over the adjacent vertices, a matching is called popular if it does not lose a head-to-head election against any other matching. Since the seminal work of Abraham, Irving, Kavitha, and Mehlhorn, who gave the first polynomial-time algorithm for finding a popular matching, numerous generalizations of the popular matching problem have been investigated. Two prominent directions are weighted popular matchings, in which each applicant is assigned a voting weight, and popularity problems under matroid constraints. The former admits a polynomial-time algorithm due to Mestre, while the most general form of the latter is the popular common independent set problem, for which a polynomial-time algorithm is given by Kavitha, Makino, Schlotter, and Yokoi.
  In this paper, we introduce the weighted popular common independent set problem, which simultaneously generalizes weighted popular matchings and popular common independent sets. Our main result is the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem. A key ingredient of the algorithm is a solution-independent characterization of weighted popular common independent sets, which we establish in this paper. As consequences of our algorithmic result, we obtain polynomial-time algorithms for several previously unresolved problems, including weighted popular matchings with matroid constraints and weighted popular branchings.

title: Online Submodular Welfare Maximization: Computation is not the Bottleneck
summary:
We revisit the online submodular welfare maximization problem (OSW), a vast generalization of numerous well-studied online allocation problems, including online bipartite matching, display ads and AdWords. A natural greedy OSW algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of $1/2$ [LLN06], and $1-1/e$ under i.i.d. arrivals [KPV13]. Both bounds are tight for polynomial-time algorithms unless NP=RP [KPV13]. The information-theoretic limits for OSW, in contrast, remained open. This prompted researchers to ask for tighter upper bounds [Mehta13] or conjecture the existence of better-competitive (slow) algorithms [Huang23, LTX+23, CHS24, Huang2024, HTW24}.
  We resolve Mehta's question and refute the subsequent conjectures, proving that the greedy algorithm is in fact tight for both adversarial and i.i.d. arrivals, regardless of computation time. Seemingly contradicting recent $(1-1/e)$-competitive fractional algorithms for OSW [HJP+24,Patton26], we show that this impossibility even holds for fractional algorithms, provided their outputs correspond to marginals that are roundable in hindsight. Conceptually, our proofs can be seen as identifying that a bottleneck for OSW, even under (deterministic) adversarial arrivals, is the inherently random notion of correlation gap [ADSY12].

title: OT-FlowRec: Optimal Transport-Guided Multi-Bridge Flow for Multimodal Sequential Recommendation
summary: E-commerce user preferences evolve dynamically within sessions, exhibiting concurrent and multi-centric interest distributions. While existing multimodal sequential recommendation methods leverage global attention to compress historical interactions, they inadequately capture the concurrent nature of multi-interest behaviors and fail to model the underlying multi-centric distribution of user intent. To tackle this issue, we propose OT-FlowRec, an optimal transport-guided multi-bridge flow matching framework that explicitly models multi-interest distributions to facilitate multimodal sequential recommendation. Unlike single-path generative models, OT-FlowRec constructs a mixture of parallel, interest-specific transport flows to model the multi-centric distribution characteristics, where each flow preserves a distinct user interest cluster via an optimal transport plan. Then, a geometric transport mechanism is designed to establish minimum-cost paths from the latent multi-interest distribution to target preference prototypes to provide multi-interest awareness. Moreover, a progressive time-sampling warmup strategy dynamically biases optimization weights toward the final states of the generation process, bridging the gap between continuous global distribution fitting and practical top-$k$ ranking metrics. This approach achieves explicit interest disentanglement, ensuring the preservation of a multi-peaked preference representation instead of collapsing it into a unimodal average. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that OT-FlowRec outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines.

title: SiteEvo: An LLM Agent for Autonomous Discovery of Site-Adaptive Massive MIMO Detectors
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Designing a massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) detector that is tailored to each specific deployment site can improve detection performance, yet most existing detectors, including deep-unfolding methods, adapt mainly within human-prescribed algorithmic structures. This letter proposes SiteEvo, a site-adaptive agentic discovery framework that extends adaptation from parameter tuning to detector-algorithm discovery. Rather than selecting or recombining predefined architectures, the large language model (LLM) agent synthesizes complete executable detector programs under a common design contract by combining its pretrained communication knowledge, site-specific wireless evidence, and experience accumulated during the search. Each proposal defines its own processing structure and trainable parameterization, and the parameters are optimized by a communication-system backend. The resulting high-performance detector is further structurally refined to reduce block-level computational cost under a bit error rate (BER)-preservation constraint and is finally frozen for deployment without online LLM inference. Simulations across three sites demonstrate BER reductions by factors of 2.6 to 6.0 over the best-performing competing detector at each site at 6 dB, while structural refinement reduces block-level computational cost by 16.7-34.1% under a validation-BER constraint.

title: Truthful Two-Facility Location with Candidate Locations in Metric Spaces
summary: We study a truthful facility location problem in which agents have private positions in a metric space and known approval preferences over two distinct facilities. Each agent incurs a cost equal to her total distance from the facilities she approves. The goal is to locate the facilities at a given set of candidate locations so as to approximately minimize either the social cost or the max cost, while incentivizing the agents to report their positions truthfully. This problem was previously studied for line metrics and deterministic mechanisms. We first settle the approximation ratio of deterministic mechanisms for the social cost on the line by establishing a lower bound of $7$, matching the upper bound from previous work, and show that randomization leads to a strict improvement. For the max cost, we show that the previously known optimal deterministic guarantee of $3$ remains tight even for universally strategyproof mechanisms. We then turn to general metric spaces. For deterministic strategyproof mechanisms, we obtain tight approximation ratios of $2n-1$ for the social cost and $5$ for the max cost. We also show that randomization yields substantial improvements for both objectives: for the social cost, we obtain a tight characterization, while for the max cost we establish nearly matching upper and lower

title: Improved Approximations for Coflow Scheduling via Iterated Rounding and Stable Matchings
summary:
We study Coflow Scheduling, introduced by Chowdhury, Zhong, and Stoica (2014). We give deterministic polynomial-time algorithms achieving a $2.77$-approximation without release dates and a $3.17$-approximation with integer release dates. These improve the $3.42$ and $4.36$ guarantees of Rohwedder and Schnaars (2025).
  Our approach combines two ideas: (1) a novel iterated rounding scheme, and (2) Galvin's list edge coloring method, which is based on the Gale--Shapley stable matching algorithm.

title: UniSGR-V2: Stepwise Target-Side Feature Anticipation and Crossing for Generative Recommendation
summary:
Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation unifies retrieval and ranking through autoregressive decoding but differs structurally from discriminative models, which can directly access rich target-item side features. The attributes are compressed into a finite codebook during quantization, while the target item remains undetermined during decoding and its features cannot be looked up. This target-side feature vacuum weakens generation at each semantic-ID level through high conditional entropy and cascading errors, and final ranking through missing target-side feature crossing.
  Existing methods interact with candidate representations or generate discrete attribute tokens, but none reconstructs a continuous target-side representation inside decoding to support both stepwise generation and ranking. We propose TacGR (Stepwise Target-Side Feature Anticipation and Crossing for Generative Recommendation). Before decoding each codeword, TacGR anticipates a continuous target-side feature vector and crosses it with the semantic prefix and user behavior sequence inside the decoder. The crossed representation conditions current-level generation and is directly used for ranking.
  Continuous-vector regression risks a learnable target collapsing with its prediction and prediction noise propagating into generation through attention. TacGR addresses these challenges with a semantic-anchoring auxiliary tower and a unidirectional visibility mask, respectively. For extremely long industrial behavior histories, it introduces gated convolutional denoising to suppress noise and adapts the pyramid memory funnel to reduce inference cost. Offline experiments on a large-scale Lazada dataset show significant gains over OneRec, UniRec, and UniSGR. Online A/B testing improves IPV, Order, and GMV by 0.79%, 5.55%, and 3.09%, respectively.

title: Rate-Distortion Theory of Gaussian Mixtures via Posterior Label Sampling
summary:
We study the mean-squared error (MSE) rate-distortion function (RDF) of finite Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) in $\mathbb{R}^d$, for which neither the RDF nor an optimal test channel is known in closed form. It can be sandwiched between the genie-aided conditional RDF $R_{\mathbf{X} | T}(D)$, which can be characterized in closed-form for a GMM, and $R_{\mathbf{X} | T}(D)+I(\mathbf{X};T)$, where $T$ denotes the latent component label. We show that the upper bound can be achieved operationally by the proposed Gibbs-relabelling method (GRM), which conveys a label from the posterior $P_{T|\mathbf{X}}$ through \textit{channel simulation} at rate $I(\mathbf{X};T)$, followed by vector quantization of the resulting exactly Gaussian conditional sources by reverse water-filling. Using the Shannon lower bound (SLB), we prove that GRM attains the SLB, and hence the RDF, of a general finite mixture if and only if every component attains its own SLB. For a GMM this holds throughout the fully active interval $D/d<\min_{k,m}λ_{k,m}$, where $λ_{k,m}$ are the eigenvalues of the component covariances, and for scalar GMMs the condition is also necessary.
  Since GRM cannot operate below the label cost $I(\mathbf{X};T)$, we propose a complementary stochastic scalar quantization (SSQ) scheme for low rates, which simulates an $M$-ary reconstruction index. We show that at low rates SSQ with $M\geq 2$ matches the Shannon RDF to first order: $R(D_{\max}-δ)=δ/(2τ^2)+o(δ)$, where $τ^2$ is a directional sub-Gaussian proxy of the mixture, and quantify the price of a finite codebook through a strict rate gap at high rates and a distortion floor whose joint scaling in $M$ and number of mixture components is characterized. Numerical results illustrate both regimes and the finite-blocklength cost of channel simulation.

title: When Does Opponent Modeling Pay Off? Spatial Inference Stabilises Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 2 algorithms, 4 tables, submitted to AAMAS 2027
summary: Deep reinforcement learning agents in partially observable competitive games must act on beliefs about an unseen opponent's intent. We study a spatial opponent model: a transformer trained with hindsight-relabelled opponent goals that outputs a subgoal heatmap from the opponent's observed trajectory, fused early into a dueling double DQN. In symmetric constant-sum foraging games with partial observability, the module stabilises training. Plain TD(0) DQN suffers degenerate seeds in three of four one-step configurations, whereas the opponent-model agent never collapses and, wherever training succeeds, recovers the majority of the symmetric game value. Transfers zero-shot to a foraging opponent unseen by the learner, with a positive goal advantage over the baseline, and loses this edge exactly where an information argument predicts: against a full-information tracking adversary whose intent is the learner itself, and on resource-dense maps where both agents saturate. A blindfold ablation, zeroing the heatmap at deployment, decomposes the advantage into two mechanisms: training-time stabilisation, which dominates where the credit assignment is hard and survives blinding on the dense map, and deployment-time inference, whose reliance shrinks as fog thins on the sparse map. We conclude that opponent-goal inference is a stability-and-transfer mechanism whose value is governed by measurable boundary conditions: visibility (fog thickness), opponent intent, and resource density.

title: Approximation algorithms via discrepancy with hard constraints
summary:
In this paper, we present a discrepancy-based approach to cost-preserving rounding under hard constraints. Starting from a feasible fractional solution, our rounding procedure preserves the designated hard constraints, never increases the linear objective, and bounds the error in the remaining constraints by the discrepancy of a suitable column-difference matrix.
  Our second discrepancy-theoretic result bounds the discrepancy of a matrix in terms of a novel column parameter, called mountain distance. This notion captures ordered structural features of a matrix which are invisible to the classical Beck--Fiala and Komlós column-norm parameters.
  We show a variety of applications of these two results. In particular, we obtain new results for min-cost unsplittable flows, bounded-turn routing in grids and tori, rainbow prefix hypergraph decomposition, and $2$-multicast scheduling.

title: Recall Begets Recall: Recurrent Memory Ranking for Personalized LLMs
summary: Memory ranking is the stage in personalized Large Language Models (LLMs) that decides which of the candidate memories returned by a retriever enter the limited context, so that the answer is grounded in the right parts of the user's history. Existing memory rankers operate in a single pass, scoring each candidate once against the raw query and cutting the ranked list at a fixed top-K. The single pass misses memories that the answer needs but that look unrelated to the query on their own, and the fixed cut ignores how many memories the query needs. To address both problems, we propose ReMind, a memory ranker that runs as a recurrent and self-terminating loop, following the cognitive theory of memory search: each recalled item joins the cue for the next recall (compound cueing), and recall stops once enough has been collected for the task (metamemory monitoring). For compound cueing, ReMind adds the top-ranked memory to the query context at each step and reranks the remaining candidates under the expanded cue, so that each recall makes the cue more specific and later steps look for what is still missing rather than for what merely resembles the query. For metamemory monitoring, a sufficiency predictor estimates at each step whether the collected memories are enough to answer the query and stops the loop once they are, so that the number of selected memories adapts to each query. Experiments on public benchmarks show that ReMind achieves the best results compared to state-of-the-art memory rankers.

title: Binary Codes Correcting Multiple Edits via Polynomial Hashing and Entropy Recycling
summary: Codes in the Levenshtein metric that can correct multiple edits (including deletions, insertions, and substitutions) have attracted a lot of attention recently owing to their application in DNA-based storage and racetrack memories. In this work, we present new techniques for designing explicit binary codes of length $n$ that correct $t$ edits with at most $(2t+1)\log n+O_t(\log\log n)$ bits of redundancy. We first propose to use a polynomial hash to construct a systematic code that corrects $t$ edits with $(4t+2)\log n+O_t(\log\log n)$ bits of redundancy. Then we observe that there are many polynomial hashes like this, some are good, some are bad. So, we propose the second technique, called entropy recycling, to use the indices of good hashes to carry information. As a consequence, we obtain a partial-systematic code of length $n$ that corrects $t$ edits with at most $(2t+1)\log n+O_t(\log\log n)$ bits of redundancy. Finally, we provide deterministic polynomial-time encoding and decoding algorithms for our code.

title: Linear Last-Iterate Convergence Rates for Optimistic Learning in Harmonic Games
summary: We prove that the last iterate of Optimistic Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (OFTRL) converges at a linear rate to a Nash equilibrium in multiplayer harmonic games. Our result holds under a mild game-regularity condition and for a large family of regularizers, including entropy, Tsallis, and log-barrier. Our analysis is based on a dual perspective of OFTRL: we prove that the interaction between optimism and the global structure of harmonic games leads to the dissipation of an energy function along the dual iterates, for which we establish tight quantitative bounds. Our result also holds for the Extragradient FTRL variant.

title: Hashrope: A Persistent Data Structure for Mechanisms of LLM Context Management
summary: Serving stacks for large language models manage context through four recurring mechanisms: incremental edits to a growing context, branching and snapshotting for tree search, identification of reusable prefixes for KV-cache reuse, and encoding of repeated segments. Each mechanism is served today by a different specialist structure. We show that all four reduce to a single persistent weight-balanced rope whose every node carries a polynomial hash of its subtree over a Mersenne prime, so that the structure supports logarithmic edits and logarithmic verified content-identity queries at the same time. We validate each mechanism with pre-registered, replicated experiments, then compare against a deployed specialist per mechanism: the Ropey editing library, a faithful PagedAttention copy-on-write block table, and the vendored SGLang radix matcher. On workloads that interleave edits with identity queries, Hashrope is net-superior to Ropey by a factor that grows without bound (369.7x at one million characters). Against the radix matcher on a live vLLM stack serving Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M on four A100 GPUs, Hashrope identifies a one-million-token shared prefix exactly and 1.20x faster, at a context length the dense engine cannot even prefill.

title: Tackling the Modality Inhibitance Effect with Wavelet-based Modality Integration in Multi-modal Recommendation
comment: Published in IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering (TKDE) 2026
summary: Harnessing rich modality features has recently gained prominence in multi-modal recommendation systems (MRSs). To delineate user modality preferences, existing works focus on modality fusion, which can be achieved via attentive summation or concatenation. In this work, we introduce the modality inhibitance effect - a phenomenon which limits existing MRSs when these models transit from dual-modal to tri-modal configurations resulting in significant performance degradation. In particular, apart from the modal-specific contamination encapsulated in the newly introduced modality, the inclusion of new features results in excessive informational redundancy, thereby severely impeding effective integration within current approaches. To address the modality inhibitance effect, we propose a new multi-scale modality wavelet (MMWave) multi-modal recommender, which aims to fully capitalize on essential modality features and suppress modal-specific noise. This is acheived by employing wavelet decomposition from a multi-scale (time \& frequency) perspective, ensuring that only essential (non-redundant) features of each modality are extracted. We then account for the latent associations between item modality features by designing a new structure-aware multi-modal graph learning module that captures high-order latent structural information pertaining to items.
